video_title: Gene Munster: $META Muse Signals The End Of "The Algorithm"
gist: Deepwater's Gene Munster tells Dan Nathan that hands-on time with Apple's Duo foldable doubled his revenue estimate to ~5% of Apple's FY27 revenue, that Meta's Muse marks an agentic-AI leap that makes today's recommendation algorithm obsolete within two years (with a real teen mental-health cost), and that Google now beats Apple for personalized AI while Uber's real catalyst is its stake in Travis Kalanick's Atoms. He also pushes back on a former Anthropic researcher's 10%-extinction warning as overstated while agreeing AI's societal impact is being under-priced.

insights.claim: After going hands-on at the launch event, Gene Munster doubled his revenue estimate for Apple's Duo foldable, now expecting it to account for roughly 5% of Apple's fiscal 2027 revenue versus his prior estimate of 2-2.5%.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A near-doubling of a new product-line revenue estimate from a well-followed Apple analyst can shift consensus modeling for FY27 — watch for other sell-side revisions to follow.
insights.quote: I think this is probably going to account for 5% of Apple's revenue in fiscal '27.

insights.claim: Munster's view flipped from 'no one will want this' to 'people will consider this' specifically because the closed device, while 14% thicker than an iPhone Pro Max at its thinnest point, hides its foldable crease almost invisibly, making it feel like two separate phones rather than a compromise foldable.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Hardware execution quality, not just specs, is the swing factor for whether a niche category (foldables, ~low single-digit % of smartphones) crosses into mainstream demand.
insights.quote: It's heavier than you think, but the thickness of it is 14% thicker.

insights.claim: It is unusual for this many sell-side analysts to revise estimates right after an Apple hardware event, but 30 of the roughly 38 analysts actively covering Apple in FactSet changed their numbers following the Duo/dual-event launch.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Above-normal analyst revision activity signals the Street sees this event as more consequential than a typical iterative hardware refresh.
insights.quote: 30 of them changed their numbers

insights.claim: Despite the flurry of analyst revisions, the absolute dollar revenue estimates among analysts who updated their models actually fell about 1%, showing the sell-side remains net skeptical of Duo's impact even as the stock rallied on the news.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A gap between a rising stock price and falling analyst dollar estimates suggests the rally is being driven by investor sentiment/multiple expansion ahead of fundamentals — a setup worth monitoring for later analyst catch-up upgrades or disappointment.
insights.quote: the absolute number the absolute dollars actually went down by 1% for the analysts that changed their estimates.

insights.claim: Analyst quarterly estimates shifted because Apple split its release cadence: December quarter growth estimates were cut from about 11% to 6%, while March quarter estimates were raised from about 12% to 18%, reflecting the new 18e/Air models launching in spring rather than the holiday quarter.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Investors modeling Apple's holiday quarter should not read a lower December growth number as demand weakness — it is a launch-timing shift, with the offset showing up in the March quarter.
insights.quote: December growth went from like 11% down to six, and then March went from like 12 to 18 or something like that.

insights.claim: The negative surprise from Apple's event was on Siri/Apple Intelligence: the new Siri is still only in English beta (unchanged since July), expanding to beta in five more languages in October within the US only, with a footnote explicitly excluding the EU and China entirely — which Munster ties to the stock selling off during the day before recovering as investors focused on Duo.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Apple's AI assistant remains geographically and functionally limited with no announced prime-time date — a continuing overhang on the 'Apple has AI chops' narrative that investors should track for a real launch date, not another beta expansion.
insights.quote: it had a footnote on there that was really small that said excludes EU and China.

insights.claim: Apple's caution on Duo's case/durability design traces back to lessons from 'Antennagate' and screen-scratching complaints, where the company learned to think through downstream physical-design failure modes before shipping — relevant now because three of Duo's four surfaces are glass.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Apple's historically conservative approach to hardware failure modes, plus Apple Upgrade Program insurance bundling, suggests durability/breakage risk for a glass-heavy foldable is likely already underwritten rather than an unpriced tail risk.
insights.quote: what it was a learning. I mean, culturally, it was a learning that they need to think about these kind of downstream effects.

insights.claim: Munster argues Apple's decision to keep the 'Siri' brand name is a mistake given its reputation for being unreliable, despite roughly 2.5 billion daily 'Hey Siri' invocations that make it one of the most-used voice interfaces in the world.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Legacy brand baggage on Siri could blunt user willingness to trust Apple's new agentic assistant even if the underlying technology improves, a soft but real headwind to Apple's AI monetization story.
insights.quote: the fact that they're keeping the Siri name, I just think is a disaster.

themes.theme: Meta Muse and the End of the Algorithm

insights.claim: Munster's central thesis is that Meta's historic recommendation engine — built on algorithmically inferring past behavior to maximize engagement — is 'junior varsity' compared to the 'professional level' step-change represented by Muse's agentic approach, and that within about two years the current algorithm-based paradigm will be effectively obsolete.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: If accurate, Meta's engagement/monetization model is about to undergo a structural upgrade distinct from any prior algorithm tweak, which could justify a re-rating independent of ad-pricing cycles.
insights.quote: The algorithm's dead. Like that that is not going to mean anything in 2 years

insights.claim: The key distinction Munster draws is that today's systems predict what you'll click based on your past behavior, while agentic systems like Muse proactively think and act on your behalf based on what they infer you'll want next.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: This reframes the AI competitive question for social platforms from 'better recommendations' to 'who owns the agent that acts for the user' — a much higher bar for engagement and monetization.
insights.quote: What they're coming out with uh is more like professional level.

insights.claim: Roughly 3.5 billion people — about half the internet-using population — use a Meta product daily, meaning even modest engagement gains from agentic AI compound across an enormous existing user base.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Scale magnifies the financial impact of any per-user monetization or engagement improvement from Muse, making even incremental agentic gains material to Meta's revenue base.
insights.quote: Half of the internet uh what is it? 3.5 billion people uh a day use a a a meta product.

insights.claim: Meta's Muse reveal revived investor interest in monetizing WhatsApp, a platform previously seen as having no demonstrated monetization plan, reflecting a shift in sentiment toward the stock after weeks of being punished for AI infrastructure spending.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: WhatsApp monetization has been a long-dormant optionality story for Meta bulls; a credible agentic product could be the catalyst that finally makes that thesis actionable.
insights.quote: we can turn on WhatsApp.

insights.claim: Munster argues Meta's pending changes tied to its teen health and wellness settlement will be largely moot because the entire algorithmic paradigm being regulated is itself being replaced by agentic AI within roughly two years.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Regulatory remedies aimed at 'the algorithm' may be targeting a technology that is already being superseded, meaning near-term settlement compliance costs could matter less than the market assumes.

insights.claim: Despite being broadly bullish on AI's net societal benefit, Munster explicitly predicts teen and general mental health outcomes will get worse specifically because of the increased engagement and utility that agentic AI like Muse will drive on Meta's platforms.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: An AI-bullish institutional investor voluntarily flagging a mental-health downside is a notable signal for ESG/regulatory risk assessments on Meta, distinct from the pure growth narrative.
insights.quote: teen health, specifically teen health is going to be is going to get worse. Mental health is going to become worse because of what we're talking about here.

insights.claim: Munster and Nathan agree Google/Alphabet is arguably the best-positioned company in AI on a vertically integrated basis, spanning Gemini, the Spark and Dream Beans consumer AI products, Gmail and the productivity suite, Android, YouTube, GCP/GPU infrastructure, and core search and advertising.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A full-stack distribution advantage across consumer touchpoints and infrastructure gives Google multiple monetization surfaces for AI, reducing reliance on any single product's success.

insights.claim: Deepwater Asset Management was a long-time Google shareholder but exited the position in part due to concerns about internal 'brain drain,' only to watch Gemini subsequently make what Munster calls remarkable improvements.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A real-money example of a professional investor selling right before an inflection point underscores how hard AI-driven turnarounds are to time, and is a caution against over-weighting narrative momentum (positive or negative) in stock decisions.
insights.quote: we were a long-time investors in Google. We're no longer investors in part because of brain drain.

insights.claim: Google search growth bottomed around 9% before Gemini-driven improvements, briefly accelerated into the low-20% range, and is now running mid-to-high teens — a stronger trajectory than feared, though not exciting enough on its own to reignite investor enthusiasm for the stock.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Search growth resilience via AI is a durable positive data point for Alphabet bulls, but the stock likely needs a headline-grabbing 'exciting at scale' product to re-rate, not just steady fundamental improvement.
insights.quote: search was growing at 9% and then I think might have even gotten in the low 20s and it's kind of hovering at mid to high high teens right now

insights.claim: Given a straight choice today between Google and Apple for personalized AI, Munster would pick Google, explicitly because Apple has not yet demonstrated comparable AI capability.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: This is a direct, quotable relative-preference call from an Apple-focused analyst that investors weighing Apple vs. Google AI exposure can use as a sentiment data point.
insights.quote: Google just because Apple has not demonstrated to me.

insights.claim: Munster flags that xAI's next Grok version, due at the end of 2026, will incorporate SpaceX engineering data, positioning it as a potentially 'incredible' entrant in industrial AI applications.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: An AI model trained on proprietary aerospace engineering data could open a differentiated industrial/enterprise AI vertical for xAI, worth tracking as a potential wedge against Google and OpenAI in specialized domains.
insights.quote: The new Grok that's going to be out at the end of this year that kind of will fully take in uh the all the engineering data within SpaceX

themes.theme: Tesla Physical AI and the Uber-Atoms Trade

insights.claim: Munster frames Uber's real near-term catalyst not as its own robotaxi rollout but as its investment in Atoms, a private company founded by Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick pursuing autonomy assistance, automated back-of-house commercial kitchens, and a mining business.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Investors screening Uber purely on ride-hailing/delivery fundamentals may be missing an underappreciated optionality catalyst in Atoms that Munster says the market hasn't priced given limited visibility into its progress.
insights.quote: The opportunity for Uber is within Atoms.

insights.claim: Tesla's Full Self-Driving intervention rate has fallen close to zero, and Tesla's NHTSA filing requesting to put 1,000 robotaxis on the road signals a level of internal confidence that Munster says contrasts with Elon Musk's more cautious public 'safety paranoia' commentary over the prior several quarters.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A regulatory filing revealing more aggressive internal deployment plans than public rhetoric suggests is a concrete, checkable signal of Tesla's true confidence in FSD safety, ahead of any public announcement.
insights.quote: they had a thousand they wanted to put a thousand of these on the road. This is based on the Nitsa filing against Tesla over the weekend.

insights.claim: Unlike smartphone adoption, which was slowed for years by carrier contracts and switching friction, Munster predicts robo-taxi/autonomy adoption could see something closer to a full 'switch flip' within the next roughly two years once trust is established.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A faster-than-typical adoption curve for autonomous ride-hailing would compress the timeline for market share shifts away from human-driven ride-hail and legacy auto ownership models.
insights.quote: on the robo-taxi side, that can be a relative switch flip over that I think the next 2 years.

insights.claim: Munster names Chrysler-Stellantis as effectively 'dead' and calls out Honda and Volkswagen as being in serious trouble as legacy automakers facing the physical-AI/autonomy transition.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A blunt relative-loser call among legacy automakers gives investors a concrete short/avoid list tied to the autonomy transition thesis, distinct from the more commonly discussed Tesla/Uber winners.
insights.quote: Chrysler-Stellantis, they're dead. Honda is in big trouble.

insights.claim: A former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher's public warning of a 10% chance of human extinction went viral largely because he forfeited unvested Anthropic stock grants to make the statement — a costly personal signal that lent it credibility beyond his individual research fame, timed just before Anthropic's IPO.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Costly signaling (forfeiting money) from insiders is a higher-credibility warning sign for AI safety risk than commentary alone, and is worth monitoring ahead of major AI-company liquidity events like IPOs.
insights.quote: why this picked up so much traction is because he stepped away from stock grants that what are going to invest in a couple months.

insights.claim: Munster interprets the researcher's substantive concern as being about recursive learning — AI systems training other AI systems — as the mechanism driving progress toward superintelligence, a state beyond artificial general intelligence where machine outputs can no longer be traced back or understood by humans.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: Recursive/self-training AI development loops are a distinct and identifiable technical risk factor investors and policymakers can track separately from generic AI-safety alarm, since it directly affects how predictable model capability gains become.
insights.quote: The machines are training the machines training the machines and this kind of path to super intelligence.

insights.claim: Munster's own position is that he does not believe human extinction from AI is a realistic near-term outcome, but he does believe the scale and significance of the AI buildout is being under-appreciated and that its rollout carries a geopolitical racing dynamic that warrants more caution.
insights.speaker: Gene Munster
insights.so_what: A measured 'it's real and under-priced but not existential' stance from an AI-bullish investor is a useful counterweight to both AI-doom and AI-hype extremes when calibrating portfolio risk around AI exposure.
insights.quote: I don't believe we're going to see the end of the world because of this.

insights.claim: Roughly $15 trillion in market capitalization, concentrated among about 20 stocks, has been created since ChatGPT's launch, underscoring how much investor capital is already riding on the AI narrative playing out.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: This scale of concentrated market-cap creation frames the stakes of the AI safety and AI-bubble debate — a meaningful pullback in sentiment could have outsized index-level effects given the concentration.
insights.quote: I think $15 trillion in market cap, probably among 20 stocks, has been gained since Chat GPT came out.
